questions.prompt: Fluid in the extracellular spaces between cells is called _____.
questions.hint: It occupies the spaces around tissue cells.
questions.explanation: Fluid becomes lymph once it enters lymphatic vessels.

questions.prompt: Interstitial fluid becomes _____ when it enters a lymphatic capillary.
questions.hint: Name the same fluid after it enters a lymph vessel.
questions.explanation: The name changes according to the fluid's compartment.

questions.prompt: Abnormal accumulation of interstitial tissue fluid producing swelling is called _____.
questions.hint: A common clinical sign of impaired fluid drainage.
questions.explanation: Lymphatic impairment can cause a specific form called lymphedema.

questions.prompt: Lipid-rich intestinal lymph transported after a fatty meal is called _____.
questions.hint: This term is different from 'chyme.'
questions.explanation: Chyle contains intestinal lipid particles, often chylomicrons.

questions.prompt: The blood-fluid protein-associated pressure that helps retain water in circulation is _____ pressure.
questions.hint: A synonym is colloid osmotic.
questions.explanation: Plasma proteins help exert oncotic pressure.

questions.prompt: Initial lymphatic capillaries begin as _____-ended pockets in the tissues.
questions.hint: Unlike a blood-capillary loop, the beginning is closed.
questions.explanation: Their blind ends are specialized for interstitial-fluid uptake.

questions.prompt: Overlapping endothelial flaps in an initial lymphatic capillary create _____-way entry of fluid.
questions.hint: The flaps favor inward rather than outward flow.
questions.explanation: Higher tissue pressure opens entry flaps.

questions.prompt: Connective-tissue _____ help prevent initial lymphatic capillaries from collapsing as tissue swells.
questions.hint: Think of tethers to surrounding connective tissue.
questions.explanation: Anchoring filaments help hold capillary lumens open.

questions.prompt: Collecting lymphatic valves prevent _____ of lymph.
questions.hint: They enforce net directional movement.
questions.explanation: Valves counter reversal during intermittent pumping.

questions.prompt: Specialized lymphatic capillaries inside intestinal villi that receive chylomicrons are called _____.
questions.hint: They appeared in the Digestive System chapter too.
questions.explanation: Lacteals carry dietary fat particles into lymph.

questions.prompt: The _____ duct returns lymph from most of the body except the right upper quadrant.
questions.hint: It is the larger of the two named lymph ducts.
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct typically terminates near the left venous angle.

questions.prompt: The right lymphatic duct receives the right jugular, subclavian, and _____ trunks.
questions.hint: The trunk draining thoracic viscera has the longest name.
questions.explanation: These are the three right upper-quadrant trunks in the lecture.

questions.prompt: The enlarged lymphatic chamber receiving the lumbar and intestinal trunks is the _____.
questions.hint: This saclike structure is near the start of the thoracic duct.
questions.explanation: It collects lymph from inferior regions of the body.

questions.prompt: The thoracic duct commonly enters venous circulation at the _____ venous angle.
questions.hint: Opposite the usual termination of the right lymphatic duct.
questions.explanation: This angle is formed by left internal jugular and subclavian veins.

questions.prompt: Lymph from the RIGHT upper limb normally reaches the right _____ trunk.
questions.hint: Its name matches the vein near which lymph returns.
questions.explanation: Ipsilateral subclavian trunks drain upper limbs.

questions.prompt: _____ lymphatic vessels carry lymph into a lymph node.
questions.hint: Think arriving rather than exiting.
questions.explanation: Afferent lymph enters through the convex side of a node.

questions.prompt: The space just beneath a lymph node capsule that receives incoming lymph is the _____ sinus.
questions.hint: Its name describes its position.
questions.explanation: Lymph enters this sinus before continuing through cortical and medullary sinuses.

questions.prompt: The lymph node _____ is enriched in T lymphocytes.
questions.hint: This deep cortex lies between outer cortex and medulla.
questions.explanation: T cells often enter from blood through high endothelial venules here.

questions.prompt: The lymph node outer cortex contains B-cell-rich lymphoid _____.
questions.hint: These structures may develop germinal centers.
questions.explanation: Follicles are organized B-cell areas.

questions.prompt: A(n) _____ center is a site of activated B-cell proliferation and maturation in secondary follicles.
questions.hint: The word also appears in the anatomy slides.
questions.explanation: Germinal centers support clonal expansion and affinity-related selection.

questions.prompt: Lymphocyte production and development is called _____.
questions.hint: Similar in form to 'hematopoiesis.'
questions.explanation: Lymphopoiesis refers specifically to lymphocyte formation.

questions.prompt: T lymphocytes mature in the _____.
questions.hint: A primary lymphoid organ in the mediastinum.
questions.explanation: Thymic selection is essential to functional self-tolerant T cells.

questions.prompt: B lymphocytes develop primarily in the _____ in humans.
questions.hint: This is also where their precursors originate.
questions.explanation: Human B-cell maturation is bone-marrow-associated.

questions.prompt: The barrier restricting exposure of immature thymocytes to circulating antigens is the blood–_____ barrier.
questions.hint: It is prominent in thymic cortical tissue.
questions.explanation: It helps maintain the proper environment for immature thymocytes.

questions.prompt: Age-associated shrinkage of the thymus is called thymic _____.
questions.hint: The thymus becomes partly replaced with fatty tissue.
questions.explanation: Involution changes thymic structure as people age.

questions.prompt: The spleen filters _____ rather than the lymph that lymph nodes filter.
questions.hint: The spleen is part of blood-borne immune surveillance.
questions.explanation: Spleen white pulp responds to antigens traveling in the blood.

questions.prompt: The _____ pulp of the spleen contains many lymphocytes.
questions.hint: This is the immune-rich splenic compartment.
questions.explanation: White pulp is associated with arterial branches and blood-borne antigen recognition.

questions.prompt: The _____ pulp removes many aged or damaged erythrocytes.
questions.hint: Think about the compartment rich in RBCs.
questions.explanation: Red-pulp macrophages filter abnormal erythrocytes.

questions.prompt: Blood enters the spleen through the splenic _____.
questions.hint: Opposite of the splenic vein.
questions.explanation: The splenic artery carries blood to be surveyed and filtered.

questions.prompt: Removal of the spleen by surgery is called _____.
questions.hint: The term ends with 'ectomy.'
questions.explanation: Loss of splenic function increases vulnerability to some encapsulated bacteria.

questions.prompt: The three encapsulated lymphoid organs named by the instructor are lymph nodes, thymus, and _____.
questions.hint: The largest lymphoid organ in the abdomen.
questions.explanation: The instructor groups these three together in the capsule comparison.

questions.prompt: The two main PRIMARY lymphoid sites are bone marrow and _____.
questions.hint: The organ where T cells mature.
questions.explanation: Primary sites are for lymphocyte formation/maturation, not merely antigen filtering.

questions.prompt: Aggregated lymphoid nodules particularly common in the ileum are called _____ patches.
questions.hint: A named intestinal immunological landmark.
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are part of GALT.

questions.prompt: Lymphoid tissue organized at mucosal surfaces is abbreviated _____.
questions.hint: The acronym has four letters.
questions.explanation: This grouping includes sites in gut and airways.

questions.prompt: The pharyngeal tonsil is also called the _____.
questions.hint: Located high in the nasopharynx.
questions.explanation: Pharyngeal tonsillar tissue is commonly called the adenoid.

questions.prompt: The instructor classifies NK-cell monitoring as immunological _____.
questions.hint: Another term for immune policing of abnormal cells.
questions.explanation: NK cells are innate lymphocytes involved in immunological surveillance.

questions.prompt: The engulfment and intracellular digestion of microbes by neutrophils/macrophages is _____.
questions.hint: Literally a cell 'eating.'
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis is a key immediate defense.

questions.prompt: NK cells and cytotoxic T cells can release perforin and _____ to help induce apoptosis.
questions.hint: Cytotoxic serine proteases.
questions.explanation: Granzymes enter target cells and activate death pathways.

questions.prompt: Programmed cell death is termed _____.
questions.hint: A controlled process, unlike uncontrolled cell rupture.
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic lymphocytes can induce apoptosis in abnormal target cells.

questions.prompt: A granulocyte rapidly recruited to many bacterial infections is a _____.
questions.hint: Common initial phagocytic responder.
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are prominent early inflammatory phagocytes.

questions.prompt: The four cardinal signs in the lecture are rubor, calor, tumor, and _____.
questions.hint: Latin for pain.
questions.explanation: The professor's list includes redness, warmth, swelling, and pain.

questions.prompt: The Latin term for swelling in an inflammatory response is _____.
questions.hint: Not automatically a cancer diagnosis in this context.
questions.explanation: Tumor in the cardinal-sign list means swelling.

questions.prompt: The Latin term for inflammatory heat is _____.
questions.hint: Related to 'calorie' and warmth.
questions.explanation: Increased perfusion contributes to warmth.

questions.prompt: Mast cells release _____, an inflammatory mediator that promotes vasodilation and vascular permeability.
questions.hint: Commonly associated with allergic reactions too.
questions.explanation: Histamine alters local blood vessels during inflammation.

questions.prompt: Circulating molecules that trigger fever are called _____.
questions.hint: They influence the hypothalamic temperature set point.
questions.explanation: Pyrogenic signaling helps produce fever.

questions.prompt: The complement fragment that coats many targets for phagocytosis is _____.
questions.hint: A cleavage product of complement component 3.
questions.explanation: C3b is a major opsonin.

questions.prompt: The terminal complement complex that can perforate membranes is abbreviated _____.
questions.hint: A three-letter acronym beginning with M.
questions.explanation: The membrane attack complex includes terminal C5b–C9 proteins.

questions.prompt: Complement-mediated coating of a pathogen to enhance phagocytosis is called _____.
questions.hint: It 'tags' a microbe for engulfment.
questions.explanation: Antibodies and C3b can act as opsonins.

questions.prompt: Type I _____ trigger antiviral defense programs in nearby cells.
questions.hint: Cytokines named for interfering with viral replication.
questions.explanation: Antiviral interferon signaling changes cellular defenses.

questions.prompt: The complement pathway often triggered by antigen-bound antibodies is the _____ pathway.
questions.hint: A pathway distinct from lectin and alternative.
questions.explanation: Antibody-mediated classical complement activation is highlighted in the lecture.

questions.prompt: MHC class _____ is recognized by CD8 cytotoxic T cells.
questions.hint: The class broadly present on nucleated cells.
questions.explanation: Class I presents peptides to CD8 T cells.

questions.prompt: MHC class _____ is recognized by CD4 helper T cells.
questions.hint: Primarily associated with professional APCs.
questions.explanation: Class II presents peptides to CD4 helper cells.

questions.prompt: The _____ T-cell subtype typically coordinates B-cell activation with cytokines and contact signals.
questions.hint: The CD4-positive subset.
questions.explanation: Helper T cells support antibody-mediated responses.

questions.prompt: A second activating signal needed by many naive T cells in addition to TCR recognition is called _____.
questions.hint: Prevents activation from an antigen signal alone in many settings.
questions.explanation: Costimulation contributes to appropriate naive T-cell priming.

questions.prompt: An antigen-specific activated lymphocyte population can increase through clonal _____.
questions.hint: Think multiplication of matching cells.
questions.explanation: Activated T or B cells proliferate into a clone.

questions.prompt: A differentiated B-cell descendant that secretes large amounts of antibody is a _____ cell.
questions.hint: Its name resembles a blood-fluid compartment.
questions.explanation: Plasma cells are antibody factories.

questions.prompt: A specific region of antigen recognized by an antibody is an _____.
questions.hint: The professor calls this an antigenic determinant site.
questions.explanation: Each antibody binding site recognizes an epitope.

questions.prompt: The antibody isotype commonly most abundant in serum is _____.
questions.hint: The isotype highlighted as a major serum antibody.
questions.explanation: IgG performs diverse systemic functions.

questions.prompt: The antibody class produced early in many primary responses is _____.
questions.hint: Often the first major secreted isotype.
questions.explanation: IgM is prominent early in the course's primary response diagrams.

questions.prompt: The antibody class common in tears, saliva, and intestinal secretions is _____.
questions.hint: Major mucosal antibody.
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA protects exposed mucosal surfaces.

questions.prompt: The antibody class most associated with immediate allergic mast-cell reactions is _____.
questions.hint: 'E' is the allergy association.
questions.explanation: IgE binding can support mast-cell/basophil degranulation.

questions.prompt: The amount or activity of specific antibody measured in serum is called an antibody _____.
questions.hint: A laboratory measure often based on dilution.
questions.explanation: Titers are commonly compared between primary and secondary responses.

questions.prompt: A response after encountering the same antigen again is called a _____ immune response.
questions.hint: The later response is often faster and stronger.
questions.explanation: Memory cells influence the secondary immune response.

questions.prompt: Protection produced by your own antigen-specific response is _____ immunity.
questions.hint: It is produced after infection or immunization.
questions.explanation: Active immunity involves recipient immune activation.

questions.prompt: Transfer of preformed antibodies from one source to another produces _____ immunity.
questions.hint: Maternal antibodies are a common example.
questions.explanation: Passive immunity can act promptly without initially eliciting memory.

questions.prompt: Human immunodeficiency virus primarily targets _____ helper T cells.
questions.hint: Number associated with helper rather than cytotoxic T cells.
questions.explanation: Advanced CD4 impairment disrupts immune coordination.
